title: Cardiovascular Changes During Pregnancy, Labour and Puerperium
path: Cardiovascular Changes During Pregnancy, Labour and Puerperium

headings.title: Introduction to Maternal Cardiovascular Adaptations
headings.content: Pregnancy places a massive demand on a woman's body, and the circulatory system undergoes profound transformations to support the growing fetus. These changes begin very early, often within the first trimester, to ensure adequate uteroplacental perfusion and meet the metabolic needs of maternal organs. Hormonal shifts, particularly surges in estrogen, progesterone, and relaxin, act as the primary drivers behind these systemic alterations. Understanding these baseline physiological adjustments helps nurses distinguish normal pregnancy signs from cardiovascular pathology.

headings.title: Hemodynamic Changes and Blood Volume Expansion
headings.content: To meet the demands of the uteroplacental unit, total blood volume increases dramatically by about 40% to 50% above pre-pregnant levels, peaking around the 32nd week of gestation. Plasma volume expands much more rapidly than the red blood cell mass, leading to a condition known as **physiological anemia of pregnancy** or hemodilution. This drop in hemoglobin concentration is not a true nutritional deficiency, but rather a beneficial dilution effect that reduces blood viscosity, easing the workload on the maternal heart and improving microvascular flow.

headings.title: Cardiac Output and Structural Heart Modifications
headings.content: Cardiac output rises early, increasing by 30% to 50% by the end of the second trimester. This elevation is achieved primarily through an increase in **stroke volume** and an elevated **heart rate**, which typically climbs by 10 to 15 beats per minute. Structurally, the heart responds to this increased volume load with mild left ventricular hypertrophy and a slight upward displacement of the apex due to the expanding uterus pushing against the diaphragm.

headings.title: Blood Pressure Variations and Systemic Vascular Resistance
headings.content: Despite the massive surge in blood volume and cardiac output, systemic blood pressure usually decreases during the first and second trimesters. This occurs because progesterone relaxes vascular smooth muscle, causing a marked drop in **systemic vascular resistance (SVR)**. Blood pressure reaches its lowest point around mid-pregnancy before gradually climbing back toward pre-pregnancy values by term. Mid-pregnancy hypotension is common and must be monitored carefully during routine antenatal visits.

headings.title: Vena Cava Compression and Postural Hypotension
headings.content: In the later stages of pregnancy, the heavy gravid uterus can compress the inferior vena cava and descending aorta when the woman lies flat on her back. This obstruction significantly reduces venous return to the heart, leading to a sharp drop in cardiac output and arterial pressure. This phenomenon is known as **supine hypotensive syndrome**. Symptoms include dizziness, pallor, cold sweats, and fainting. Nurses must always encourage pregnant women past twenty weeks gestation to rest and sleep in the lateral recumbent position, preferably on the left side.

headings.title: Cardiovascular Adaptations During Labour and Delivery
headings.content: Labour places intense physical stress on the cardiovascular system. With every uterine contraction, blood is squeezed out of the intervillous space of the placenta and forced back into the maternal systemic circulation, causing a temporary spike in cardiac output and blood pressure. Pain, anxiety, and muscular exertion further elevate heart rate and blood pressure during the first and second stages of labour. Careful monitoring of maternal vitals during contractions helps midwives identify early signs of cardiovascular distress.

headings.title: Cardiovascular Adjustments in the Immediate and Late Puerperium
headings.content: Following delivery of the placenta, the removal of the low-resistance placental bed causes a sudden increase in systemic vascular resistance. Simultaneously, the elimination of vena caval compression and the re-autotransfusion of blood from the uterus cause an immediate surge in stroke volume and cardiac output postpartum. Over the first two weeks, diuresis and diaphoresis rapidly eliminate the excess fluid volume accumulated during pregnancy, returning cardiac output and blood volume to pre-pregnant levels by roughly six to twelve weeks postpartum.

headings.title: Clinical Implications and Nursing Assessment for Midwifery Practice
headings.content: Midwives must be skilled at evaluating cardiovascular status across all stages of childbearing. A normal physical assessment may reveal physiological signs that mimic heart disease, such as a soft systolic murmur, peripheral edema, and mild resting tachycardia. However, severe shortness of breath, chest pain, syncope, or persistent jugular venous distension are abnormal and require immediate medical referral. Regular blood pressure checks and careful assessment of lower limbs prevent overlooked complications like pre-eclampsia or deep vein thrombosis.
